title: Rh System, Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn, and the Direct Antiglobulin Test
summary: The Rh system, especially the D antigen, is the most immunogenic red cell antigen group after ABO. This lesson covers Rh nomenclature and genetics, weak D testing, prevention and pathophysiology of Rh hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDFN), and how the direct antiglobulin test (DAT) documents in vivo red cell sensitization.
objectives: Describe the genetics and nomenclature of the Rh system and the immunogenicity of the D antigen.
Explain how weak D typing is interpreted differently in donors versus recipients.
Outline the pathophysiology, laboratory findings, prevention, and treatment of Rh hemolytic disease of the newborn.
Perform and interpret the direct antiglobulin test and distinguish IgG from complement coating.

highYield: The D antigen is the most immunogenic red cell antigen after ABO; anti-D is usually IgG, crosses the placenta, and reacts at AHG phase.
Rh-negative individuals lack D antigen and can form anti-D after exposure to D-positive red cells through transfusion or pregnancy.
RhIg (anti-D immunoglobulin) prevents immunization of Rh-negative mothers carrying an Rh-positive fetus; it is given antenatally and postpartum per protocol.
The DAT detects antibody or complement bound to red cells in vivo; it is positive in HDFN, hemolytic transfusion reactions, and autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
Classic teaching: weak D donors are treated as Rh-positive (their cells can immunize); weak D recipients are treated as Rh-negative (to avoid giving D antigen to a potential anti-D former).

rows: Treat as Rh-negative (give Rh-negative red cells)
Manage as Rh-negative per local policy; RhIg may be indicated
Interpret with DAT and maternal history

quickReview.mnemonic: DONORS are positive, PATIENTS are negative when weak D — donors can DONATE the D immunogen; patients must be PROTECTED.

deepStudy.introduction: After ABO, the Rh system causes the most clinically significant immunohematology problems. The Rh genes RHD and RHCE encode membrane proteins carrying multiple antigens, of which D is the most important because of its strong immunogenicity. An Rh-negative (D-negative) patient who receives D-positive red cells, or who carries a D-positive fetus, can form anti-D, an IgG antibody capable of causing delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions and hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn. The laboratory's jobs are to type donors and patients accurately (including weak D variants), to detect and identify anti-D when it forms, to support obstetric care with RhIg prophylaxis, and to use the antiglobulin test to prove when red cells have been sensitized in vivo.

sections.heading: Rh genetics, nomenclature, and immunogenicity
sections.body: The Rh system is encoded by two highly homologous genes, RHD and RHCE, on chromosome 1. The Wiener nomenclature uses Rh-Hr symbols (R1, R2, r, and so on), while the Rosenfield numeric system labels antigens D, C, c, E, e. The D antigen is carried on the RHD gene product; individuals who are Rh-negative usually lack RHD entirely (most commonly through a deletion in European-ancestry populations, though other molecular mechanisms exist in African-ancestry populations, producing partial D phenotypes). D is highly immunogenic: a single transfusion of D-positive red cells immunizes a meaningful proportion of D-negative recipients, and small fetal-maternal bleeds during pregnancy or delivery can do the same. Anti-D is predominantly IgG (usually IgG1 and IgG3), does not bind complement efficiently enough to cause severe intravascular hemolysis on its own, reacts optimally at AHG phase, and crosses the placenta readily. Clinically significant IgG Rh antibodies generally cause extravascular hemolysis in the spleen and liver. The C, c, E, and e antigens are less immunogenic but clinically important; anti-c in particular is a common cause of HDFN after anti-D has been prevented.

sections.heading: Weak D and partial D: typing and clinical handling
sections.body: Some red cells type as D-negative with immediate spin anti-D but react weakly with antiglobulin reagent; historically these were called Du, now termed weak D. Weak D results from reduced numbers of D antigen sites on the cell surface, often due to RHD variant genes. The clinical handling rule is asymmetric: weak D donor units must be labeled and issued as D-positive, because even a small dose of D antigen can immunize a D-negative recipient; weak D recipients or patients are treated as D-negative and receive D-negative red cells, again to prevent immunization. In obstetrics, a weak D pregnant patient is generally managed as Rh-negative, with RhIg considered per local policy. Modern molecular RHD genotyping can distinguish weak D types (for example types 1, 2, and 3, which are typically not immunogenic) from partial D phenotypes that may form anti-D; many reference laboratories now use genotyping to guide RhIg decisions, but routine serologic practice in many centers still follows the conservative rule. Partial D patients can form anti-D against the D epitopes they lack, which is why partial D is not simply equated with D-positive in every context.

sections.heading: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN)
sections.body: HDFN occurs when maternal IgG antibody crosses the placenta and binds antigen-positive fetal red cells, causing extravascular hemolysis. Rh (anti-D) HDFN classically affects a second or later D-positive fetus of a sensitized D-negative mother: a small fetomaternal hemorrhage during the first pregnancy sensitizes the mother, and subsequent pregnancies with a D-positive fetus face an anamnestic antibody rise. Severity ranges from mild neonatal jaundice to hydrops fetalis and intrauterine death. ABO HDFN, by contrast, is usually mild because IgM anti-A and anti-B do not cross the placenta well and fetal A/B antigens are poorly developed; it most often occurs in group O mothers with IgG anti-A,B and can affect a firstborn. Laboratory evaluation includes maternal antibody screen and titer, paternal or fetal antigen typing (or cell-free fetal DNA where available), amniotic fluid bilirubin monitoring (delta OD450), middle cerebral artery Doppler peak systolic velocity, and cord blood testing: ABO/Rh typing, DAT, hemoglobin, and bilirubin. Prevention with RhIg (anti-D immunoglobulin) given to D-negative, unsensitized mothers during pregnancy and after delivery (and after any sensitizing event) has made severe Rh HDFN uncommon; RhIg must be given before sensitization occurs and is ineffective once anti-D is established. Treatment of affected newborns includes phototherapy, exchange transfusion, and, in utero, intravascular transfusion.

sections.heading: The direct and indirect antiglobulin tests
sections.body: The direct antiglobulin test (DAT) asks whether the patient's red cells are already coated in vivo with IgG and/or complement (usually C3d). Patient red cells are washed to remove unbound immunoglobulin, then mixed with polyspecific AHG containing anti-IgG and anti-C3; agglutination indicates coating. Monospecific AHG reagents identify whether the coating is IgG, C3, or both, which narrows the differential: warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia is usually IgG, cold agglutinin disease is usually C3, drug-induced reactions vary, and HDFN due to IgG anti-D shows IgG-coated cells. A positive DAT does not by itself prove hemolysis; it proves sensitization, and clinical and laboratory correlation (bilirubin, haptoglobin, LDH, reticulocytes, smear) is required. The indirect antiglobulin test (IAT), used in antibody screens, crossmatch, and antibody identification, detects unbound antibody in serum: reagent red cells are incubated with patient serum, washed, and tested with AHG. False-negative DATs occur with low-affinity or low-density coating and technical errors such as inadequate washing; false positives occur with hypergammaglobulinemia and complement activation during collection. The DAT is central to the workup of HDFN, suspected hemolytic transfusion reactions, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and drug-induced immune hemolysis.

deepStudy.clinicalSignificance: Anti-D and other Rh antibodies cause delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions and HDFN. RhIg prophylaxis is one of the great success stories of transfusion medicine, but it only works when the laboratory correctly identifies D-negative patients (including weak D handling) and when the product is given on time. In the transfusion service, a positive antibody screen with anti-D means the patient must receive D-negative, antigen-negative blood, and crossmatch-compatible units must be selected accordingly.
deepStudy.labInterpretation: Interpret D typing in clinical context: donor vs patient vs obstetric. Correlate DAT results with monospecific typing and hemolysis markers. Antibody titers (for anti-D in pregnancy) are reported as the reciprocal of the highest dilution showing agglutination; critical titer thresholds vary by laboratory and method, and management is guided by local obstetric protocols and serial titers plus ultrasound findings, not by a single number. Reference intervals and critical values must be verified against your local laboratory's procedure manual.

examTraps: Weak D donor units are issued as Rh-positive, but weak D patients receive Rh-negative blood — the rule flips depending on whether you are looking at a donor or a patient.
A positive DAT means the cells are coated in vivo; it does not automatically mean hemolysis is occurring, and a negative DAT does not fully exclude an antibody-mediated process.
RhIg prevents sensitization; it does not treat an already sensitized mother and will not lower an established anti-D titer.

memoryHooks.text: Weak D: DONORS are positive, PATIENTS are negative — donors can donate the immunogen, patients must be protected from it.
memoryHooks.funny: Weak D donor = tsinelas na dapat itago (positive!). Weak D patient = dapat alagaan (negative!). Don't mix them up — hindi ito jowa na pwedeng palitan.

memoryHooks.text: Think of RhIg as a bodyguard given to an Rh-negative mom so her immune system never 'meets' the D antigen and never remembers it.
memoryHooks.funny: RhIg: parang chaperone sa date — para hindi ma-in love ang immune system ni mommy kay baby D. Prevention is better than sensitization, charot.
